lesson.title: What's a Bank?
lines: A bank is like a giant, super-strong safe for your money. In Zedville, every citizen banks at Universal Bank.
A bank helps people and businesses to:
• Keep money safe — your money is protected in your account
• Pay and move money — paying bills, buying things and sending money to others
• Borrow money — a loan has to be paid back, usually with interest
Three things you can do with your account:
• Deposit — putting money into your account
• Withdraw — taking money out of your account
• Transfer — moving money to another account, for example to a friend

lesson.title: Your Universal Bank Account
lines: Your current account is your everyday account: your salary arrives here and your bills are paid from here.
• Direct deposit — City Hall sends your salary straight into your account on payday (money in)
• Auto-debit — a company you've authorised takes an agreed amount on a set date, like your School Fees (money out)
• Emergency Fund Account — a separate savings account; 20% of your salary moves into it every month and it earns interest
• Monthly statement — a list of all the money that came in and went out, and your balance
Check your statement every month and make sure you recognise every transaction.

lesson.title: What's a Budget?
lines: A budget is a plan for your money. It helps you:
• Know your money — how much is coming in
• See where it goes — what you spend it on
• Plan to save — set some aside for things you want later

library_modules.title: Tracking Income & Expenses
library_modules.changes: Q3 and Q10 in the original were the same question with the same answers, and Q1/Q6 overlapped. Replaced with surplus/deficit questions and the student's own statement. The lesson now explains surplus and deficit.

lesson.title: Income and Expenses
lines: Income is the money you receive. In Zedville, your main income is your monthly salary, paid by direct deposit. In real life, income can also come from:
• Allowance from parents
• Gifts
• Jobs, like babysitting or dog walking
• Selling things you no longer need
Expenses are the things you spend money on:
• Needs — things you must have for daily life and school, like meals, School Fees and transport
• Wants — things that are nice to have but you could live without, like games, treats or designer clothes
Savings are not an expense: instead of spending the money, you set it aside for later.

lesson.title: The Flow of Money
lines: Income flows in and expenses flow out. Comparing the two tells you where you stand:
• Surplus — income is bigger than expenses, so you have money left to save
• Balanced — income and expenses are the same
• Deficit — expenses are bigger than income, so you're spending money you don't have
Your bank statement shows every amount that came in and went out. Track your spending — small purchases add up!

lesson.title: What is an Emergency Fund?
lines: An emergency fund is money you save for unexpected problems — like when your phone breaks, your pet gets sick, or your family gets a surprise bill.
How big should it be? Aim for 3 to 6 months of your living expenses.
• Security — a cushion when something goes wrong
• No debt — you can pay for surprises without borrowing
Your Emergency Fund Account at Universal Bank grows by 20% of your salary every month and earns 2% interest per year.

lesson.title: Building It with the 50-30-20 Rule
lines: • 50% Needs — essentials like School Fees, lunch, transport and bills
• 30% Wants — things you enjoy, like games, treats or movie tickets
• 20% Savings — including your emergency fund and other goals
Keep it somewhere safe that you can reach quickly — like a bank savings account, not under your mattress.
Only use it for real emergencies: unexpected, necessary and urgent. If you use some, build it back up.

library_modules.title: Simple Interest
library_modules.changes: Removed the three questions about the “money seed”, “gardener” and “growth boost” analogy (they tested the story, not the maths). Added the formula, calculations, and the compound-interest trap (121 zeds). Uses Universal Bank's real rates.

lesson.title: What is Simple Interest?
lines: When you keep savings in a bank, the bank pays you a little extra for keeping your money there. That extra money is called interest.
Simple interest is always worked out on the amount you first saved — the principal.
Example: you save 100 zeds at 10% simple interest per year.
• After 1 year: 10% of 100 = 10 zeds of interest, so you have 110 zeds
• After 2 years: another 10 zeds, so you have 120 zeds
• The interest is the same 10 zeds every year, because it's always based on the original 100 zeds

lesson.title: Working It Out
lines: Simple interest = principal × rate × time (in years)
• Principal — the money you saved
• Rate — the percentage the bank pays per year
• Time — how many years your money stays saved
At Universal Bank, the Emergency Fund Account pays 2% per year and the Money Market Account pays 4% per year. Save more, or save for longer, and you earn more interest.

lines: • Manual payment — you start each payment yourself: paying cash, using the Pay Bills page, or tapping your card
• Debit payment — paying with a debit card or phone; the money comes straight out of your bank account, so you can only spend what you have
• Auto-debit (also called direct debit) — you authorise a company to take an agreed amount on a set date every month. Great for regular bills like School Fees, internet or subscriptions.
Remember: direct deposit = money in (your salary). Auto-debit = money out (your bills).

lesson.title: Keeping Track of Your Payments
lines: Every payment shows up on your monthly bank statement.
• Keep a record of what you pay and when
• Compare your records with your statement — this is called reconciling
• Ask the bank about anything you don't recognise — it could be a mistake or fraud
Paying on time avoids late fees and keeps your budget on track.

library_modules.title: Fixed vs Variable Expenses
library_modules.changes: The original asked “what are variable expenses?” three different ways (Q6, Q8, Q9). Merged into one and added planning questions: budgeting a variable cost from past months and choosing what to cut.

lesson.title: Fixed Expenses
lines: Some expenses cost the same amount every time. These are fixed expenses — you can count on them.
• School Fees — the same amount every month
• A monthly bus pass
• A subscription for a game or streaming app
Fixed bills are perfect for auto-debit, because the amount doesn't change.

lesson.title: Variable Expenses
lines: Other expenses change from week to week. These are variable expenses.
• Snacks — it depends on how hungry you are
• Entertainment — movies or games cost different amounts each time
• Gifts — it depends on who you're buying for
You can predict fixed costs exactly; for variable costs, plan a sensible amount and stay flexible. And remember: fixed doesn't always mean “need”, and variable doesn't always mean “want”.
